issues.legal_issue: A condemned person may obtain commutation when an unjustified delay in carrying out the death sentence causes prolonged mental agony.
material_facts: The death sentence had been confirmed through the judicial process.
The condemned person’s mercy petition remained undisposed of for more than eight years.

The delay was attributed to waiting for the decision on a co-accused’s mercy petition, which itself remained unattended for years; the Court found no sufficiently commensurate justification for the delay.

A prison visit report described the condemned person’s mental state as such that he might commit suicide if a decision was not taken soon, and the Court found that he had suffered prolonged mental agony under the shadow of death.
issues.conclusion: The death sentence should not be carried out and was altered to imprisonment for life.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 21, the Court may consider undue delay in execution after the death sentence has been finally confirmed and, having regard to the nature of the delay and all the circumstances, direct that the sentence be altered to imprisonment for life. In Sher Singh v. State of Punjab, the Court rejected a fixed two-year rule previously stated in T.V. Vatheeswaran v. State of Tamil Nadu. Smt. Triveniben v. State of Gujarat reaffirmed that the delay and its circumstances must be assessed in each case. The Court also relied on the recognition in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab that death remains an available punishment for murder; the issue here was the later delay, not the validity of that punishment generally.

rule.if: death_sentence_delay_proceeding and delay_after_final_confirmation and unjustified_mercy_delay and prolonged_mental_agony

predicates.death_sentence_delay_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to seek relief because execution of a death sentence has been delayed.
predicates.delay_after_final_confirmation: The delay occurred after the death sentence had been finally confirmed through the judicial process.
predicates.unjustified_mercy_delay: The mercy process remained pending for a prolonged time without a justification commensurate with that delay.
predicates.prolonged_mental_agony: The condemned person suffered prolonged mental agony while awaiting the outcome under the shadow of death.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns delayed execution of a finally confirmed death sentence, an unjustified mercy delay accompanied by prolonged mental agony results in commutation to life imprisonment.

issues.legal_issue: No fixed period of delay determines whether execution of a death sentence should be carried out or the sentence altered.
material_facts: The condemned person’s mercy petition had remained pending for more than eight years after the judicial process had confirmed the death sentence.
The Court considered the reasons for the delay, the repeated failure to deal with the mercy petitions, and the mental agony suffered by the condemned person.
issues.conclusion: The Court must assess the nature of the delay and all the circumstances of the case; no fixed period of delay is decisive.
issues.legal_principle: Sher Singh v. State of Punjab rejected the fixed two-year threshold stated in T.V. Vatheeswaran v. State of Tamil Nadu. Smt. Triveniben v. State of Gujarat confirmed that the Court examines the nature of the delay and the circumstances that arose after final judicial confirmation. Article 21 informs that assessment.

predicates.death_sentence_delay_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to seek relief because execution of a death sentence has been delayed.
predicates.delay_after_final_confirmation: The delay occurred after the death sentence had been finally confirmed through the judicial process.

issues.definition: In a proceeding concerning delay after final confirmation of a death sentence, the delay is assessed on the circumstances of the particular case.

issues.legal_issue: The requirement of promptness in criminal justice applies to the disposal of a condemned person’s mercy petition as part of the protection of life and liberty.
material_facts: The mercy petitions concerning the condemned person remained pending for years, with the government repeatedly leaving a related petition unattended.
The condemned person remained under sentence of death during the prolonged pendency and suffered mental agony.
issues.conclusion: Speedy trial is part of the fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, and the same principle is important for the disposal of a mercy petition.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 protects life and liberty through fair and reasonable procedure. The Court stated that speedy trial, though not necessarily a distinct fundamental right, is implicit in Article 21 and that this principle is no less important for disposal of a mercy petition. In Sher Singh v. State of Punjab, the Court stressed that the executive must act fairly and quickly and identified a three-month self-imposed guideline for disposal of mercy petitions.

predicates.condemned_person_mercy_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a mercy petition made for a person under sentence of death.
predicates.mercy_petition_pending_for_prolonged_per: The mercy petition remained undecided for a prolonged period.

issues.definition: When a condemned person’s mercy petition remains pending for a prolonged period, prompt disposal is required as part of the protection of life and liberty.

issues.legal_issue: A proceeding concerning delay in execution after final confirmation of a death sentence does not permit the Court to reopen the judicial conclusions that confirmed the sentence.
material_facts: The death sentence had been confirmed by the High Court and the Supreme Court before the proceeding seeking relief for delay was brought.
The relief sought concerned the subsequent delay in execution and the pending mercy process.
issues.conclusion: The Court may examine the nature of the delay and the circumstances after final confirmation, but has no jurisdiction in that proceeding to reopen the conclusions reached when the death sentence was finally maintained.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 32, the Court may examine undue delay in execution of a death sentence after the judicial process has finally confirmed it, but its review is confined to the delay and the circumstances that followed confirmation. Smt. Triveniben v. State of Gujarat states this limitation; the Court also relied on T.V. Vatheeswaran v. State of Tamil Nadu and Sher Singh v. State of Punjab in addressing delay in execution.

predicates.article_32_death_sentence_delay_proceedi: A proceeding under the constitutional remedy is brought to seek relief for delay in executing a death sentence.
predicates.death_sentence_finally_confirmed: The death sentence was finally maintained through the judicial process before the delay proceeding was brought.

issues.definition: When a constitutional proceeding concerns delay after a death sentence has been finally confirmed, review is limited to the subsequent delay and circumstances.
